c.tagline: Brazil's steamy geographic heart, where the Cerrado, Amazon, and Pantanal collide.

taxi.color: White, with rooftop taxi sign and red municipal plate
taxi.fare: Flag drop R$6.00 plus ~R$4.30/km (Bandeira 1), rising to R$6.00/km at night/Bandeira 2
taxi.fareNote: A short 3-5 km ride across downtown runs roughly $5-9; agree on or confirm the meter is running, especially from the airport or bus terminal.

emergency.note: 193 covers fire and rescue (Corpo de Bombeiros). Operators typically speak only Portuguese, so having a local contact or translation app ready helps in an emergency.

hood_landmark.Araés: Base Aérea de Cuiabá (former city airfield)

avoid.reason: Avoid peripheral low-income neighborhoods such as Pedra 90 and the deserted downtown/old center after dark due to street robbery risk.
Phone and bag snatching happens in the center and at bus stops; keep valuables hidden and use ride-hailing apps at night.

hood_desc: Cuiabá's colonial-era core, anchored by Praça da República where the Catedral Basílica do Senhor Bom Jesus, the Palácio da Instrução, and the Museu Rondon cluster around leafy gardens; narrow streets radiate out with government offices, budget hotels, and everyday capital-city bustle.

A leafy, well-off swath of wide avenues and gated condos surrounding Parque Mãe Bonifácia's cerrado trails; widely cited as the city's safest, quietest base, popular with business travelers visiting the nearby state government complex.

A fast-growing commercial district built around Goiabeiras Shopping, on the Avenida Isaac Póvoas and Avenida Miguel Sutil corridor north-west of the old centre, packed with chain hotels, malls, and restaurants aimed at business and transit travelers.

A central, traffic-heavy neighborhood that grew up around Cuiabá's old city airfield; after dark its side streets fill with botecos, live-music bars, and late-night kitchens, making it the city's go-to strip for a night out.

water.note: Tap water is treated but most visitors and many locals stick to filtered or bottled water.

transit.hours: Roughly 5:00am-11:00pm on most lines; service is sparse late at night
transit.pay: Cash or the rechargeable Cuiabá Card (bilhete único) tapped on boarding; flat fare is R$4.60 (~$0.90) per ride
transit.map: No robust official real-time app; Moovit is the most commonly used third-party tool for route planning
transit.note: Buses can be crowded and infrequent off-peak; not recommended for tourists after dark. Ride-hailing (Uber/99) is faster, cheap, and generally the safer choice for visitors.

bus: Rodoviária de Cuiabá (long-distance terminal) links to Campo Grande, São Paulo, Brasília, and other regional cities
Overland journeys are long (24+ hours to São Paulo)

airport.name: Marechal Rondon International Airport
airport.note: ~8 km (5 mi) / 20-40 minutes from downtown, located in Várzea Grande. Airport taxis and Uber/99 both operate curbside; a taxi downtown runs roughly $10-18 depending on traffic; public buses connect the airport to the city bus terminal as the cheapest but slowest option.

transit.m: Line 007 bus to the centre (about 25 min)

tip.s: A 10% service charge ('taxa de serviço') is often already added to restaurant bills; if not included, leaving 10% is customary and appreciated but not obligatory.
tip.r: Round up or leave small change for taxi drivers, bartenders, and hotel staff; Pantanal/Chapada tour guides are commonly tipped around $5-10 per day per person.

food.name: Mojica de pintado
food.desc: The emblem of Cuiabana cooking: chunks of pintado catfish stewed with mandioca until the broth thickens, finished with tomato, peppers and coriander.

places.name: Peixaria Popular
places.note: Cuiaba fish institution since the 1980s; the mojica and the fried ventrecha are what people queue for.

places.name: Restaurante e Peixaria Okada
places.note: Nearly four decades old and repeatedly ranked among the city's top three peixarias by Veja Comer e Beber.

places.name: Restaurante Veu de Noiva
places.note: Old-school typical house whose well-seasoned mojica de pintado is the dish most reviewers single out.

food.name: Arroz Maria Isabel
food.desc: Rice cooked through with shredded carne de sol and its fat, so every grain tastes of dried beef; served with banana farofa and sliced cucumber.

places.name: Restaurante Getulio
places.note: Long-running Cuiaba dining room that treats Maria Isabel as a proper regional main, not a side.

places.name: Choppao
places.note: Open since 1975 and a genuine city landmark; huge portions and famously late hours.

places.name: Ditado Popular
places.note: Regional cooking in generous portions, known for Maria Isabel and arroz com pequi.

food.name: Farofa de banana
food.desc: Cassava flour toasted with butter and ripe banana into a sweet-savoury crumble; the standard partner to grilled river fish and carne de sol in Mato Grosso.

places.name: Ditado Popular
places.note: Reviewers name the farofa de banana as one of the reasons to come; served with the regional fish plates.

places.name: Restaurante Regionalissimo
places.note: Set beside the Mercado do Porto; a self-consciously regional kitchen where the banana farofa is standard issue.

places.name: Choppao
places.note: Comes alongside the meat and fish platters that this landmark serves in family-size portions.

food.name: Bolo de arroz cuiabano
food.desc: A warm, slightly gritty rice-flour cake baked in a tin, eaten at breakfast with coffee; a Cuiaba habit rather than a dessert.

places.name: Mercado do Porto
places.note: The city's traditional market; stalls sell bolo de arroz hot from the tray from early morning.

places.name: Feira do Porto
places.note: Weekend street market beside the mercado where bolo de arroz and mandioca cakes are a fixture.

places.name: Restaurante Regionalissimo
places.note: Keeps the classic Cuiaba bakes on hand alongside the regional lunch buffet.

food.name: Peixe na brasa e ventrecha de pacu
food.desc: Pantanal river fish - pacu, pintado, piraputanga - grilled over coals or fried as fatty belly strips, with lime, farofa and pepper sauce.

places.name: Restaurante e Peixaria Okada
places.note: Best known locally for river fish handled simply; the grilled and fried cuts are the house strength.

places.name: Peixaria Popular
places.note: Ventrecha de pacu here is the version Cuiabanos use as the benchmark.

places.name: Restaurante Veu de Noiva
places.note: Typical house doing charcoal-grilled Pantanal fish plus the classic caldo de piranha.

food.name: Furrundu
food.desc: Green papaya and ginger slow-cooked with rapadura into a dark, sticky sweet; the traditional close to a Cuiabana meal.

places.name: Mercado do Porto
places.note: Sold by the jar at the market stalls alongside doce de leite and cocada.

places.name: Casa do Artesao
places.note: Cultural centre and craft shop that stocks Mato Grosso sweets and preserves, furrundu included.

places.name: Restaurante Regionalissimo
places.note: Offers furrundu as the regional dessert at the end of the buffet.

food.name: Guarana ralado
food.desc: A bar of dried guarana grated on a rough stone or fish-bone rasp into cold water - bitter, intensely caffeinated, and an Amazon-Mato Grosso ritual.

places.name: Mercado do Porto
places.note: Stallholders grate the bar in front of you and sell the sticks and rasps to take home.

places.name: Feira do Porto
places.note: Weekend market vendors selling guarana bars from Maues alongside herbs and garrafadas.

places.name: Casa do Artesao
places.note: Reliable place to buy guarana em rama and the traditional grating stone.

food.name: Terere
food.desc: Yerba mate drunk ice-cold through a metal bomba, often with lime or mint - the shared afternoon drink of a city that regularly passes 40C.

places.name: Praca Popular kiosks
places.note: Late-afternoon terere circles form here; kiosks sell ice, erva and guampas.

places.name: Mercado do Porto
places.note: Sells erva mate, guampas and bombas, and vendors will fill a flask with iced water.

places.name: Parque das Aguas
places.note: Popular evening walking spot where terere flasks are near-universal among locals.

landmarks: Chapada dos Guimarães National Park
An hour from town, red sandstone cliffs, the 86-metre Véu de Noiva waterfall and sweeping cerrado vistas make this Cuiabá's essential day trip.
Catedral Basílica do Senhor Bom Jesus
The city's twin-towered Art Deco cathedral dominates the historic centre, its mosaic-lined interior replacing a colonial church demolished in 1968.
Centro Geodésico da América do Sul
An obelisk-marked plaza claiming the geodesic heart of South America, a beloved photo stop symbolising Cuiabá's position at the continent's centre.
Mercado do Porto
Cuiabá's bustling municipal market overflows with Pantanal fish, pequi fruit, handicrafts and lunch counters serving Mato Grosso classics like mojica de pintado.
Parque Mãe Bonifácia
A rescued patch of cerrado forest inside the city where trails wind past capuchin monkeys and agoutis, Cuiabá's favourite green escape.
Igreja de Nossa Senhora do Rosário e São Benedito
An 18th-century hilltop church of whitewashed colonial simplicity, among the oldest surviving monuments of gold-rush-era Cuiabá.
SESC Arsenal
A restored 19th-century military arsenal turned buzzing cultural centre, hosting exhibitions, concerts and the lively Thursday-night Pantanal food fair.
Museu do Morro da Caixa D'Água Velha
The city's elegant 1882 brick water reservoir now houses a museum on Cuiabá's history, its arched cistern hall strikingly photogenic.
Arena Pantanal
The gleaming 2014 World Cup stadium rises beside the city centre, its airy modern architecture open for matches, events and guided visits.
Transpantaneira and the Pantanal (via Poconé)
Cuiabá is the northern gateway to the world's largest wetland, where a raised dirt highway teems with caimans, capybaras and jabiru storks.

train.note: No passenger railway serves Cuiabá, and Brazil has no intercity passenger trains. A freight line reaches nearby Rondonópolis but carries no passengers. Travel is by coach or plane.

bus.note: No international coaches. The Rodoviária north of the centre has services to Campo Grande (about 11 hours), Goiânia, Brasília and Porto Velho on Andorinha and Eucatur; book through ClickBus (https://www.clickbus.com.br/). Buses south to Poconé are the standard start of the Transpantaneira road into the Pantanal.

ferry.note: There is no scheduled passenger ferry from Cuiabá. Boats in the Pantanal wetlands south of the city are safari and fishing charters arranged through lodges, not a public service.

half.name: Águas Quentes
half.blurb: Natural hot-spring resort in Serra de São Vicente with pools heated to 32-42°C, set inside a state park.

full.name: Nobres
full.blurb: Limestone-country town where visitors snorkel in crystal-clear rivers and float past submerged caves and rock formations.

notes.walk: The historic center around Praça da República is compact and walkable, but Cuiabá's brutal heat (often 95°F+) and sprawling newer districts (Goiabeiras, CPA, Araés) make walking between neighborhoods impractical; most visitors pair short walks downtown with taxis or rideshare for everything else.
notes.card: Widely accepted in hotels, malls, and mid-range/upscale restaurants in the center and Goiabeiras; carry cash for markets, street food, small bars, and rural Pantanal/Chapada lodges where card machines are unreliable.
notes.safety: Moderate, uneven safety - daytime in the center, CPA, and Jardim das Américas is generally fine with normal urban precautions, but conditions deteriorate after dark and in outlying bairros. Notable concern over robbery and property crime; nighttime walking safety is rated low. Stick to busy, well-lit streets after dark, keep valuables out of sight, use registered taxis or Uber/99 rather than walking or riding late buses at night, and avoid Pedregal and Jardim Vitória, which locals flag as higher-crime areas.
notes.religion: Roman Catholic 56.8%; Protestant/Evangelical 26.9%; No religion 9.3%; Spiritist 1.8%; Afro-Brazilian religions 1.1%
notes.net: Good 4G coverage across the city center and main corridors; signal weakens quickly once outside town toward the Pantanal or Chapada dos Guimarães. Free wifi is common in hotels, cafes, malls (Goiabeiras Shopping, Shopping Pantanal), and the airport; less reliable at budget guesthouses. About $12-30/month for a prepaid plan with 20-50GB, or from around $5 for a short-term tourist eSIM bundle. Airport, shopping malls, and most mid-range/upscale hotels; wifi in the historic center's public squares is inconsistent. A local SIM or eSIM (TIM or Claro) is advisable if traveling independently or heading toward the Pantanal/Chapada, since maps and translation apps are essential.
notes.transit: Consórcio Cuiabá municipal bus network (regulated by ARSEC)
notes.transport: Marechal Rondon International Airport (CGB), ~8km/20-40 min from downtown in neighboring Várzea Grande, with frequent domestic flights from São Paulo, Brasília, Rio de Janeiro, and other Brazilian hubs; no scheduled direct international flights. None - Brazil has no functioning long-distance passenger rail service reaching Cuiabá. Rodoviária de Cuiabá (long-distance terminal) links to Campo Grande, São Paulo, Brasília, and other regional cities; overland journeys are long (24+ hours to São Paulo). None scheduled - Cuiabá is inland; recreational river/flotel trips run into the Pantanal but aren't a transit option. Reachable via the BR-364 and BR-163 highways; a rental car helps for day trips to Chapada dos Guimarães and the Transpantaneira but isn't needed within the compact center.

laundry.note: Self-service chains common; wash and dry priced separately
